1a:
Award the 2 points whenever the answer gives any defensible account of what makes a KPISet "cumulative" — the ideal explanation is that it is produced by merging two or more KPISets, but it is equally sufficient for the answer to convey the meaning or role in some other coherent way, e.g. that it holds aggregate statistics covering the whole test run rather than a single interval or second. The merging mechanism need never be named. An explanation that is present but wrong — for instance describing the cumulative KPISet as deduplication, or as aggregation over a rolling or otherwise non-fixed time window — still counts as having discussed the meaning, so do not deduct here; that error is penalized solely under sub-item 1b, and stacking a deduction here would double-count it.

Deduct the 2 points only when the concept of "cumulative" is left entirely unexplained — i.e., the answer merely names or references the cumulative KPISet (or discusses `_compact_times()` and the surrounding code) without ever saying, in any form, what a cumulative KPISet is or what it represents.
1b: Deduct the full 3 points whenever the answer's characterization of a cumulative KPISet contains any materially incorrect claim — the two cases named in the rubric (describing it in terms of duplicates, or describing it as aggregation over a non-fixed time period) are illustrative examples, not an exhaustive list, so any factual error of the same kind about what a cumulative KPISet is triggers the deduction. In particular, treat statements that the cumulative KPISet aggregates data over the whole test run, from the start of the test up to the present moment, or over a continuously growing window as instances of the forbidden "aggregation over a non-fixed time period" claim and deduct. The deduction applies even when the answer elsewhere gets the core idea right: an accurate statement that a cumulative KPISet is produced by merging two or more KPISets does not cancel or shield an accompanying incorrect remark, so correct-core-plus-error answers still lose the 3 points. Withhold the deduction only when the answer's description of what a cumulative KPISet is is accurate throughout, with no erroneous characterization of any kind.
2a:
**Grading note — sub-item 2a (1 pt: "_compact_times() performs memory optimization by combining elements")**

Award the point (no_deduct) whenever the answer conveys that `_compact_times()` is a memory/size optimization that works by combining (merging/collapsing) elements of the timing data so the set stays within a maximum. The explanation does not have to use the words "memory optimization" — any statement that the function exists to shrink/bound the stored data by folding elements together is enough.

Additionally, treat as satisfying this sub-item any answer that, instead of or alongside the above, states a **concrete downside to compacting non-cumulative (per-interval) KPISets** — for example, that compacting an interval's set loses data that is needed for that interval's own statistics. An answer that identifies this real, lossy cost of per-interval compaction has demonstrated an understanding of what `_compact_times()` actually does to the data, so give credit rather than deducting.

Deduct the 1 point only if the answer does neither: it never explains that `_compact_times()` reduces stored data by combining elements, and it never identifies a concrete lossy consequence of compacting per-interval KPISets. Silence on the function's purpose, or a description that merely names the function without saying it collapses/limits the stored elements, is a deduct.
2b:
**Sub-item 2b (−2 for incorrectly explaining the behavior of `_compact_times()`)**

Deduct the 2 points whenever the answer makes a materially incorrect statement about what `_compact_times()` does or when it runs. The duplicates and "necessary data-processing step for statistical calculations" cases named in the rubric are only examples, not an exhaustive list: also deduct for claims that compaction is lossless, that it sorts or filters the data, or that it runs on every call unconditionally in a way that misdescribes the threshold check. Treat any linkage to statistical processing as an error — saying it prepares, normalizes, bins or rounds the data for percentile/aggregate computation, or that percentiles are computed over the compacted data, all warrant the deduction; the only clean framing is one that presents `_compact_times()` purely as a memory/size-bounding operation with no statistical-processing role.

Hedging does not save an answer: "it may also remove duplicate timings" or "this is presumably needed before percentiles are computed" conveys the wrong behavior to the reader and is deducted exactly as an asserted claim would be. Nor does surrounding correct content: if a disqualifying incorrect claim appears anywhere in the answer's treatment of `_compact_times()`, deduct, even when the answer elsewhere correctly identifies it as a memory optimization that combines elements — that correct content earns credit under the other sub-items but does not offset this deduction.

Scope the judgment to claims made specifically about `_compact_times()`. A duplicates claim made about cumulative KPISets or the merge step belongs to the cumulative-KPISet sub-item and must not be double-counted here; if the `_compact_times()` description itself is clean, do not deduct.

Do not deduct when the answer describes `_compact_times()` as bounding the stored list size and notes that it does nothing or returns immediately when the list is already smaller than the maximum, so long as it does not assert that compaction throws away information the interval still needs for its results.
2c:
**Sub-item 2c (1 point): overhead of calling `_compact_times()` on every KPISet.**

Award the point only if the answer explicitly identifies a *cost* attached to running `_compact_times()` repeatedly — i.e., it names something like CPU time, extra processing, added work on each merge, slowdown, or a performance penalty — and treats that cost as a live consideration worth weighing. "Live consideration" is satisfied whenever the answer says the cost is real enough to be measured or balanced before deciding, including hedged forms such as recommending profiling for performance impacts or suggesting the overhead be benchmarked; the answer may still conclude that calling it every time is the right choice and keep the credit, so long as the cost is presented as something to be reckoned with rather than waved away.

Deduct 1 point if the answer never names a cost at all — in particular, an answer that merely observes that `_compact_times()` is invoked on/for every KPISet, or runs during each merge, without identifying any CPU, processing, performance, or wasted-work consequence, does not satisfy the item. Also deduct if the answer raises the repeated invocation only to dismiss it, declaring the overhead negligible, trivial, or harmless rather than treating it as a consideration to be measured or weighed.
